dominant_offer_patterns.pattern: AI readiness, workflow audit and use-case prioritization
dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong: UAE procurement study makes clear needs assessment the most influential factor; MoIAT reports 91% clarity after assessment and 95% action on recommendations.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Make a defined discovery product the entry offer, with artifacts the buyer owns: workflow map, baseline, build-vs-buy decision, data/privacy risks, prioritized roadmap and fixed implementation quote.

dominant_offer_patterns.pattern: Proof of concept or one contained workflow before scaling
dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong: DMCC cites a successful PoC as a winning selection factor; DEWA describes step-by-step scaling; MoIAT recommends validating PoCs before plant-wide scale.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Sell a measurable pilot with explicit success/failure gates, not an open-ended transformation engagement.

dominant_offer_patterns.pattern: Document intelligence and internal knowledge assistants
dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong: DEWA reduced BRD production from one week to one day; DMCC automated document processing and expense verification; AD Ports uses agents for procurement, compliance, policy answers and claims documents.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: This is the best evidence-backed initial build offer for broad UAE operations teams.

dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong at enterprise level: DEWA's Rammas handled 9.2 million inquiries; official UAE guidance explicitly identifies automated customer-service queries. SME WhatsApp demand still needs direct customer-language validation.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Position around response time, bilingual coverage, verified answers, CRM handoff and human escalation—not 'chatbots'.

dominant_offer_patterns.pattern: System-connected AI agents and workflow automation
dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong: AD Ports describes agents for repetitive work, container planning, claims, investment-review groundwork and everyday drafting; integration and measurable business goals recur across buyer evidence.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Lead with one workflow and named integrations, with monitoring and exception handling.

dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Medium-to-strong: DMCC explicitly required bilingual interactions and robust cloud security; UAE PDPL creates real data-handling obligations. Direct SMB evidence for willingness to pay extra for Arabic remains incomplete.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Treat bilingual UX and privacy controls as delivery requirements and proof points, not decorative claims.

dominant_offer_patterns.pattern: AI training, workshops and change management
dominant_offer_patterns.buyer_evidence: Strong for enterprise adoption: DEWA used champions and phased training; the UAE procurement study recommends knowledge-transfer sessions and employee training.
dominant_offer_patterns.implication: Bundle enablement into deployments; a standalone generic workshop is crowded unless tied to a written roadmap and specific workflows.

buyer_selection_language: Start with a clear needs assessment and requirement definition.
Show a working proof of concept using real or representative business data.
Integrate with the systems already in use: Microsoft 365, Teams, SharePoint, CRM, ERP, portals and mobile apps.
Define measurable success before build: handling time, response delay, error rate, documents processed, adoption, cost per case or revenue-stage movement.
Provide human review and escalation for uncertain or high-stakes outputs.
Explain data flows, consent, access, retention, deletion, security and UAE PDPL alignment.
Support Arabic and English where customer or employee journeys require it.
Make build-vs-buy, vendor lock-in, change management, training and ongoing support explicit.
Use phased rollout and earn the right to scale.

differentiation_gaps: Most competitors list technologies; few show the current manual workflow, baseline, acceptance test and human escalation path together.
Many claim UAE compliance; few publish a plain-English data-flow and PDPL delivery checklist.
Arabic is frequently asserted but rarely demonstrated with dialect, RTL, evaluation and human-review detail.
Public price transparency is uncommon and inconsistent; a narrow fixed-scope first engagement can reduce buyer uncertainty.
Many local case-study pages use anonymous or unverifiable examples. Named customer proof with a baseline, timeframe and metric would be a major trust advantage.
There is room for integration-first pages organized around Microsoft 365/Teams/SharePoint, WhatsApp, CRM and ERP rather than model names.
There is room for an explicit 'we may recommend no AI' diagnostic that produces a portable written decision.

stripe_risk_review.verdict: A truthful UAE AI consultancy/custom software offer is not itself prohibited or restricted on Stripe's current UAE list. Approval is not guaranteed; Stripe evaluates the actual business, owners, bank details, fulfillment and risk. The website must match the services declared in the account.
safe_core_positioning: custom business software and AI applications
data integration, training and ongoing technical support
avoid_or_require_separate_review: Building or selling AI for gambling, adult sexual content, illegal goods, document falsification or deceptive get-rich-quick schemes
Acting as a payment facilitator, marketplace merchant of record, money transmitter, exchange or escrow provider
Crypto exchanges, wallets, mining or staking services without Stripe approval
Investment, brokerage, lending, mortgage, real-estate investment or other regulated financial services
Telemedicine, prescription delivery or regulated medical-device sales
Unlicensed government-service resale, misleading government claims, identity-theft protection, private investigation or surveillance-heavy services
IT consulting or cloud services supplied to prohibited jurisdictions/persons, including the Russia-related restrictions stated by Stripe
website_controls: Say exactly what the company sells today; do not imply a shipped SaaS product if none exists.
Use service checkouts/payment links only for defined deliverables or invoices; do not accept money on behalf of clients or future third-party sellers.
Publish legal company identity, UAE address, working email/phone, pricing or quote mechanics, delivery timeline, refund/cancellation policy, privacy policy and terms.
Avoid guarantees such as fixed ROI, guaranteed approval, guaranteed leads or medical/financial outcomes.
Screen projects and clients against Stripe restrictions before issuing a payment link.
